Aubergine.
DIFFICULTY
Tricky
4/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Aubergines are decorative, heat-loving relatives of the tomato, grown for their glossy fruits as well as their purple flowers and large velvety leaves. They can crop well under glass or in a warm polytunnel, but outdoors they are a gamble except in very warm, sheltered places. The key requirement is heat: cool, grey weather slows growth and often delays fruiting until late summer. Treat aubergines as tender annuals, give them rich soil, steady moisture without waterlogging, and harvest the fruits while the skin still has its shine. Fruits may be oval, round or long, and varieties range from the familiar dark purple to white, violet and striped forms.

Key risks
Red spider mite

Pale mottling appears on upper leaf surfaces, with tiny mites beneath.

Slugs

Aphid

Aphids gather on young leaves and shoots.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
16
FRUITING CROPS

Warmth is the first requirement.

A greenhouse or polytunnel is the most reliable UK setting.

Pick while the skin is glossy.

Waiting for dull, seedy fruit reduces quality and further cropping.

Soil & preparation
Use rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil or peat-free compost in a sunny, sheltered position. Add mature compost before planting.
Under cover, use one plant per 12 in. pot or two per standard growing bag; avoid cold, sodden roots.
Sowing & planting
Raise in warmth
Plant into warmth
Sow indoors 

Use seed compost and keep at 70°F or warmer. Buy young plants if you cannot provide steady heat.

Prick out and pot on 

At the first true leaves, move seedlings into individual pots. Give them warmth and good light. Pot on as the roots fill the pot.

Plant out 

Wait until the soil is warm before planting. For an outdoor crop, harden off first and shelter the plants with cloches until settled. Water in gently.

Looking after the crop
Keep plants warm and ventilate on damp days. Water more in heat, less in cool weather. Avoid waterlogging.
Stake stems and tie loosely. Pinch tips for bushy growth if the variety needs it. For large fruit, remove new flowers once five or six fruits have set. Let pollinators in on warm days.
Feed with organic potash feed as fruit swells. Check early for mites and whitefly so biological controls have time to work.
Harvesting & storage
Cut the fruit while glossy, before the skin dulls and seeds harden.
Pick regularly until cold nights slow growth.
At the end of the season, chop or shred healthy woody stems before composting.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Red spider mite	Pale leaf mottling; mites beneath.	Check undersides; use suitable predatory mites early.
Whitefly	White flies beneath leaves; sticky deposits.	Identify early. Use biological control under glass.
Slugs	Low fruit and young plants are chewed.	Keep fruit raised; inspect and hand-pick around vulnerable plants.
Aphid	Colonies on shoots and young leaves.	Squash damaging clusters and encourage predators.
Mould	Grey mould in damp, stagnant conditions.	Remove infected material; improve airflow and avoid wet foliage.
Verticillium wilt and Phytophthora blight	Persistent wilting; roots or stems may decay.	Confirm the cause. Remove affected plants and avoid infected soil.
Final tips

Buy sturdy spring plants if warm, bright propagation space is unavailable.

Thin fruit to suit the variety and desired size; no single count fits all.

Beet, Leaf.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Leaf beets suit gardeners who enjoy spinach but find it quick to bolt or difficult in dry weather. Swiss chard, seakale beet, spinach beet and perpetual spinach are grown for leaves and stems; a few plants give repeated harvests over a long season. Chard has broad leaves and thick, edible midribs in white, red, yellow or pink, making it attractive in a flower border. Spinach beet has plainer green leaves, used like spinach. Pick regularly: young leaves are tender for salads or cooking, while oversized leaves toughen and growth slows. In mild winters, established plants may give an early-spring flush before flowering.

1 in.

Recommended varieties
Bright Lights

A colourful chard selection with stems in several shades. Harvest young leaves for salads or larger leaves and stems for cooking.

Rhubarb Chard

Red stalks and dark leaves make this chard decorative as well as useful. Treat it as a red-stemmed type unless a cultivar is specified.

Spinach Beet

A leaf beet grown for repeated picking of green leaves. Useful as a cooking green through a longer season than true spinach.

Fordhook Giant

A white-stemmed chard with broad green leaves. A useful kitchen choice when leaf yield matters more than mixed stem colours.

Lucullus

Pale stems and crinkled green leaves. Pick the outer leaves regularly for a continuing crop.

White Silver 2

Broad green leaves and white, fleshy stalks. Useful for both leafy greens and cooked stems.

Key risks
Slugs

Leaf beet is usually hardy and trouble-free, but slugs may nibble young plants, especially in autumn or damp weather.

Manganese deficiency

Yellowing between leaf veins can indicate a nutrient problem, but symptoms overlap.

Leaf spot

Leaf spots may have pale brown centres and dark brown or purple margins, roughly 1/4 in. across.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
24
SALADS & LEAVES

Keep leaves growing steadily.

Rich soil, regular picking and reliable moisture give tender leaves.

Choose the type for your kitchen.

Chard gives colourful stems; spinach beet is grown mainly for its leaves.

Soil & preparation
Grow in fertile soil with compost or well-rotted manure, avoiding waterlogged ground.
Chard tolerates a wide range of conditions, while spinach beet prefers cool, moist weather and a deep, fertile soil.
Sowing & planting
Sow seed clusters
Thin young plants
Sow 

Place the corky seed clusters 1 in. deep in rows 18 in. apart. Keep the seedbed moist. Each cluster can produce several seedlings.

Looking after the crop
Thin for mature leaves or baby-leaf picking, leaving the strongest seedlings. Weed regularly, especially while plants establish; cut off early flower stems to prolong cropping.
Water in dry spells and mulch to conserve moisture. Steady moisture and regular picking encourage fresh, tender leaves.
Harvesting & storage
Gently twist or pull outer leaves downwards without disturbing the roots. Leave the young centre to feed the plant and keep growing; never strip it bare.
Use small leaves in salads. Larger leaves are edible but tougher; cook them and thick chard midribs separately if needed. Start midribs first, as they take longer to cook.
Overwintered plants can give an early spring picking before they flower. In a mild winter this second flush may last a month or two before flowering stems appear.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Bolting	Flower stems rise; leaf production declines.	Remove early flower stems; replace plants once flowering persists.
Slugs	Young leaves and seedlings are chewed.	Check young plants after dark; hand-pick and protect establishment.
Downy mildew	Yellow patches above; grey-purple mould below.	Remove diseased leaves; thin promptly and improve drainage.
Manganese deficiency	Yellowing between veins; margins may curl.	Check drainage and soil pH; avoid over-liming and confirm the cause.
Leaf spot	Brown-centred spots with darker borders.	Remove affected leaves and debris; rotate and avoid crowding.
Final tips

Pick a little from several plants to keep a supply of young leaves coming.

Keep late sowings growing before winter; they may provide useful early spring leaves.

Beetroot.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Beetroot’s sweet, earthy roots suit raw salads, hot dishes, pickles, borsch and chutneys; young leaves are edible too. This cool-climate crop needs well-drained, humus-rich soil and steady moisture. Growth starts slowly, then roots swell quickly. Sow small batches for summer, autumn and storage crops. Lift before roots become woody or leathery. In mild winters some can stay outside, but severe frost can freeze and rot them.

Key risks
Bolting

ROOT CROPS

A cool-climate crop.

Use well-drained soil rich in organic matter.

Keep moisture steady.

Drought hardens roots; sudden wet can split them.

Sow for a long season.

Successive sowings extend the harvest.

Raise in warmth
Set the final plant
Sow indoors

36
ROOT CROPS

Prepare the soil well.

Deep, fertile, stone-free and sandy soil is ideal.

Avoid fresh manure.

Follow a crop manured the previous year.

Weed young seedlings.

Weeds can easily smother them.

Soil & preparation
Use deep, fertile, sandy, stone-free soil; choose short-rooted varieties on heavy or stony ground. Improve clay well before sowing.
Follow a previously manured crop. Avoid fresh manure, which encourages forking; lime acid soil in winter and prepare a fine seedbed.
Sowing & planting
Sow thinly
Cover lightly
Thin later
Sow 

Wait if the soil is cold or wet. Make shallow drills 1.3 cm deep and 15 cm apart, watering them first if dry. Sow very thinly; mixing the seed with dry sand can help. Cover with fine soil or compost and keep moist while the seeds germinate.

Extend the season 

Use short-rooted varieties for early or late crops. Early and later sowings need cloches or a sheltered spot.

Thin crowded seedlings to 5–8 cm apart in damp weather or in the evening. Water dry soil first, firm afterwards and clear the thinnings to avoid attracting carrot fly.
Weed seedlings carefully; avoid hoeing close to established roots or loosening their soil.
In dry spells, soak evenly to root depth; light sprinkling is ineffective. Heavy watering after drought can split roots.
Keep young beds bare against slugs; clear early weeds before later sowings.

Lift small carrots from June; baby roots may take eight weeks. Ease with a fork to limit disturbance.
Lift storage crops around October, earlier if carrot fly appears or before hard frost and very wet weather. Slow-growing late-autumn roots risk slug and maggot damage and splitting.
Trim leaves about 1.3 cm above the crown. Store sound roots separately in sand, cool, ventilated and just above freezing; they may keep until March.

Bitterness

Stress, including uneven moisture or temperature, can increase bitterness.

Mildew

FRUITING CROPS

Keep roots warm and evenly moist.

Cold, wet compost checks young plants; avoid both drought and waterlogging.

Check the variety’s flower instructions.

Sowing & planting
Sow on edge
Handle gently
Sow indoors 

Sow one seed on edge in a 4 in. pot at about 70°F. Water as the compost begins to dry. Protect the fragile roots when moving the seedling on.

Plant in the greenhouse 

Set well-rooted plants into pots, growbags or prepared mounds once the house stays warm. Water in gently and keep water off the stem base.

Prepare a mound 

For the traditional bed method, prepare a compost-rich station about 6 in. deep and 1 ft wide.

Soil & preparation
Rich, moist, drained compost; use fresh if border soil is suspect.
Provide warm, humid air with ventilation. Avoid stagnant conditions and cold, sodden roots.
Looking after the crop
Train up a string or cane. Stop or turn the leader at the roof. Prune sideshoots for the variety, allowing one or two upper shoots to trail if space permits.

Cut fruit before it yellows and the seeds harden. Picking often encourages new cucumbers.

Endive.
DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn / Winter

Endive is a cool-season salad plant with more flavour and bitterness than lettuce, though less of lettuce's crispness. It can be eaten raw in mixed salads or cooked, and both curly-leaved frisée types and broader-leaved Batavian or escarole types are useful. Curly endive is usually for late-summer and autumn cutting, while broad-leaved endive is easier to grow for good hearts and is more useful in autumn and winter. The crop needs moisture, humus and some protection from heat or harsh frost; blanching, or choosing self-blanching varieties, gives paler, milder hearts. Small late-summer sowings can provide leaves and hearts into winter, with suitable protection in cold weather.

Key risks
Slugs

Slugs can damage seedlings and blanched endive hearts in cool, damp weather.

Bolting

Cold while young, drought and other growth checks can cause endive to flower prematurely.

Rotting

Pale hearts can rot quickly in damp conditions.

Frost

Hard frost can damage hearts.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
52
SALADS & LEAVES

Keep endive cool and moist.

Heat and dry soil encourage bitterness and premature flowering.

Blanch only a few dry plants.

Check hearts often and cut promptly once they become pale.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil. A cool, moist position helps keep the leaves tender.
Improve sticky clay with well-rotted compost so it stays open without drying out. Use an organic feed if fertility is poor.
Give late crops a sunny position. Spring and summer crops may need light shade in hot weather to avoid heat and drought checks.
Sowing & planting
Sow
Thin
Sow 

Make short, shallow drills and sow thinly in small batches. Cover with fine soil and firm gently. Start early crops under cover and protect young plants from chilling.

Looking after the crop
Thin gradually from the first true leaves. Leave 2 in. for baby leaves. Give broad-leaved heads more room than curly ones.
Hoe young plants and water thoroughly in dry weather. Weeding eases once leaves cover the soil. Shade spring/summer crops in hot spells: heat and drought check growth and encourage bolting.
Blanch well-developed, dry plants by loosely tying their leaves or covering with an opaque pot. Block drainage holes to exclude light.
Blanch a few plants at a time for about two weeks, longer in cool weather. Check often for slugs and cut pale hearts before they rot.
Harvesting & storage
Cut mature heads with a sharp knife. Use blanched hearts promptly before browning or rot develops.
Curly types suit late summer and autumn; broad-leaved types extend autumn and winter picking. Outer leaves can also be picked as needed.
Before hard frost, lift late plants with soil around their roots. Keep cool and frost-free; use promptly. Check regularly and remove decaying leaves.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Slugs	Seedlings and blanching heads are chewed.	Check under covers; hand-pick and harvest ready heads promptly.
Bolting	Plants flower after chilling, drought or other checks.	Avoid chilling young plants; keep moist and shade in heat.
Rotting	Pale hearts soften in damp conditions.	Blanch only dry plants in small batches; cut when ready.
Frost	Hard frost spoils the hearts.	Protect late crops or lift whole plants to frost-free shelter.
Aphid	Greenfly gather on leaves and hearts.	Tolerate small colonies; squash damaging clusters, favour predators.
Final tips

Sow small batches about three weeks apart to avoid a glut.

Blanch a few plants at a time; eat pale hearts at their best.

Finish blanching late plants in soil-filled boxes in dark, frost-free shelter.

Do not tie or cover wet leaves: trapped moisture encourages rot.

Keep endive cool and moist.

Heat and dry soil encourage bitterness and premature flowering.

Blanch only a few dry plants.

Sow
Thin
Sow

Sow

White rot affects onions, shallots, garlic and leeks.

Allium leaf miner

Adult flies make distinctive rows of small white feeding punctures on allium leaves.

Rust

Orange pustules appear on allium leaves, especially leeks and garlic.

Birds or frost lifting cloves

Cloves lifted by birds or frost.

Plant healthy cloves in good drainage.

Named planting stock gives a more predictable crop than kitchen bulbs.

Lift and dry bulbs at maturity.

Careful handling and thorough drying help garlic keep.

Soil & preparation
Choose an open, sunny site with fertile, well-drained soil. Add compost or well-rotted manure, but avoid stagnant winter wet.
A compost top-dressing helps retain moisture; keep it clear of emerging shoots.
Sowing & planting
Set a clove upright
Cover the clove tip
Plant cloves 

Break up a healthy bulb just before planting. Use the largest outside cloves. Set each with its point upwards, cover the tip and firm the soil.

On wet ground 

Start cloves individually in modules under cover. Plant out the rooted cloves when the bed is workable.

Keep weeds down through winter and spring. Slow winter shoots are normal: cold can check visible growth until roots and leaves grow strongly in spring.
Water roots in dry weather while bulbs grow; stop as mature foliage yellows. Cut tender hardneck scapes once buds form. Use tender scapes raw or cooked. Softneck garlic normally produces no flower stalk and usually stores longer than hardneck types.

Summer / Autumn

Oriental leaves are quick salad and stir-fry crops, mostly brassicas: Chinese cabbage, leaf radish, mibuna, mizuna, mustards, pak choi and shungiku. Many give baby leaves within a month. Plant out

Key risks
Flea beetle

Flea beetles make small round holes in young brassica leaves, especially during warm, dry weather.

Slugs

Bolting

VEGETABLE GUIDES
70
SALADS & LEAVES

Keep leaves tender.

Water regularly and avoid checks to growth.

Choose the right season.

Late-summer sowings suit most oriental brassica leaves.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil, with plenty of mature compost.
Clear earlier crops promptly and rake a fine seedbed. Keep late-summer sowings moist as they establish.
Sowing & planting
Raise small plugs
Keep the crown clear
Sow 

Use shallow drills or broadcast thinly for baby leaves. Use the depth for each type in Quick facts. Sow small batches. Give pak choi and Chinese cabbage more room when growing whole heads.

Plant out 

Raise seedlings in modules where pests or weeds make outdoor sowing difficult. Move plants before the roots are crowded. Keep the rootball intact and the crown clear. Water in well.

Looking after the crop
Water, weed, and thin or harvest crowded plants for fast, tender growth. Mesh susceptible brassicas against flea beetles and butterflies; late July/August sowings usually suffer less than spring/early summer.
Water Chinese cabbage generously and mulch around established plants, keeping centres clear. Let hearts form naturally.
Handle fragile-rooted pak choi gently; take small, regular pickings and remove damaged outer leaves. Keep ground clean against slugs. Pick shungiku shoots before flowering.
Harvesting & storage
Cut tender baby leaves about 1¼ in. above soil, keeping the growing point intact; water for regrowth. Cut rather than pick mibuna.
Pick individual leaves or whole plants according to the crop. Cut Chinese cabbage once hearts form, before damaging frost.
Mizuna and hardy mustards can give protected winter pickings. Leaf radish quality declines as winter approaches unless protected.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Flea beetle	Small round holes in young leaves.	Mesh brassica seedlings; keep growth steady.
Slugs	Chewed leaves, especially pak choi.	Hand-pick slugs; clear damaged outer leaves.
Bolting	Early flowering; poor leaves or hearts.	Sow in the right season; avoid drought and checks.
Cabbage caterpillars	Chewed leaves; eggs or larvae.	Cover with mesh; remove eggs and caterpillars.
Dryness and checks	Coarse leaves; poor hearts.	Water thoroughly, thin and mulch established plants.
Cabbage root fly	Tunnels in brassica roots.	Use mesh after sowing and rotate brassica crops.
Root disturbance	Plants loosen during picking.	Support pak choi while picking; handle roots gently.
Frost	Leaves damaged by cold weather.	Harvest tender heads; protect hardy winter leaves.

Use close sowings for baby leaves; give hearts more room.

Small late-July and August batches spread autumn picking.
